newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Analysts eye Kredietbank nestegg ahead results.
newsitem.headline: Analysts eye Kredietbank nestegg ahead results.

text.p: Belgian Kredietbank is seen reporting first-half earnings growth of 10 to 15 percent after the close of trade on Thursday.

Analysts were generally cool on the banking shares, in light of an upcoming capital issue at Generale Bank and a planned partial bourse listing of CCB, but Kredietbank was still seen as one of the most attractive shares in the sector, partly because of its large hidden reserves.
Forecasts for group net profit ranged from 6.4 to 6.7 billion francs from 5.84 billion in the first half of 1995.
One analyst forecast a 21 percent rise to 7.1 billion.

Kredietbank is the last major bank to report earnings. First-half earnings rose 18 percent to 5.1 billion francs at Banque Bruxelles Lambert (BBL), 8.6 percent to 7.31 billion at Generale Bank and on Wednesday publicly-owned CCB reported earnings jumped 41 percent to 5.41 billion,
The wide divergence between earnings growth at Generale Bank and CCB -- respectively the country's number one and two banks -- shows just how easy it is for banks to massage their numbers.
While Generale Bank revised its provisions sharply upwards, CCB chose to write back some.
"In a good economic environment, banks can produce whatever profit they want. They can forecast trouble and then provision for it," said Mignon Hanart Declerck's Stephane Roffler.
Banks also have considerable leeway in the extent to which they report capital gains on their bond portfolios.
The result of this is that many banks have considerable hidden provisions and latent capital gains, which forces analysts to look beyond bottom line earnings figures.
"Kredietbank has more hidden reserves than BBL and Generale, because of its long-standing tradition of high provisions, and that shows up in its better Tier two ratio," Roffler said.
At the end of 1995, Kredietbank's Tier two ratio stood at 5.10 percent, against 4.81 for Generale Bank and 4.31 for BBL.

Under BIS capital adequacy standards, at least half of the eight percent of capital required to be set against risk weighted assets must consist of equity and disclosed reserves. This is called the Tier one ratio. Tier two also includes undisclosed reserves and general provisions against loan losses -- in other words, banks' hidden cash stash.
Kredietbank is also seen benefiting from the fact that its shares will get a 3.75 percent higher weighting in the Brussels bourse's Bel-20 index on September 20.

This should at least minimise the impact of Generale Bank's 15 billion franc capital increase later this month and the partial privatisation of Credit Communal/Gemeentekrediet (CCB) in November, which is expected to raise about 30 billion francs.
Bank shares are set to suffer as portfolio managers adjust their holdings to the new paper.
The one shadow hanging over Kredietbank another row with the taxman, which is potentially damaging to its corporate image.

After a conflict with the Belgian tax authorities over tax liabilities involving its Irish subsidiaries in 1994, the bank was again embarrassed by media reports in August about an alleged tax avoidance scheme involving its Kredietbank Luxembourg sister bank. It has taken libel action against some Belgian newspapers.
The Irish tax conflict was settled last year, allowing the bank to write back provisions it had booked for it.
Analysts said they did not expect any impact on earnings from the Luxembourg affair.
